latin.2649: LXVII. Porro ex iis quae hactenus exposita fuerunt, colligere promptum est Remonstrantes, & Theologos confessionis Augustanae, circa doctrinam de gratia sufficienti atque efficaci, methodo quidem & dicendi formulis aliquatenus differre, sed quoad summam rei inter eos esse consensum. Nempe negant Augustanae confessionis Theologi gratiam recte dividi in efficacem & sufficientem, id affirmant autem Remonstrantes, & distinctionem illam maxime probant. Verum Theologorum confessionis Augustanae mens non est illis qui Verbum Dei audientes non convertuntur, ex parte Dei aliquod auxilium deesse sine quo converti non possunt; adeoque gratiam quae ipsis datur & offertur, minime sufficere ad fidem & poenitentiam ipsis ingenerandam. Contra enim asserunt gratiam quae offertur ipsis incredulis & impoenitentibus, mereri nomen non solum sufficientis, sed efficacis quoque: quoniam ex se efficax est ad ipsos, nisi ultro obicem ponere pergant, ad resipiscentiam & fidem adducendos.
latin.2650: LXVIII. Contra vero Remonstrantes non ideo gratiam distinguunt in sufficientem atque efficacem, quod putent gratiam quam accipiunt illi qui increduli manent, & in peccatis perseverant, non habere vim & efficaciam necessariam & praerequisitam ad hoc, ut sequatur in illis conversio, ac propterea solum nomen sufficientis, non vero etiam efficacis mereri. Agnoscunt enim illos qui Evangelium sibi praedicatum respuunt, nullo carere auxilio ad concipiendam fidem necessario; sed ideo solum gratiae cujus sunt participes denegant efficacis nomen, quod effectum ad quem destinatur in iis reapse non producat, propter impedimentum quod illi ponunt homines ejusmodi, non ipsi gratiae vis & efficacia necessaria desit.
latin.2651: LXIX. Utrique ergo fatentur & docent gratiam quae datur illis qui Evangelio parere renuunt, satis virium habere ad ipsos convertendos, & propterea solum effectum suum in illis non sortiri, quod motibus ejus resistant, & voluntarie obicem illi ponant. Ex adverso vero fideles & qui serio ad Deum convertuntur, potuisse si libuisset, gratiae quae in ipsis efficax est, obicem ponere, & effectum ejus impedire sua contumacia, neque per eam gratiam ullam ipsis fuisse necessitatem impositam credendi, & se ad Deum convertendi.
latin.2652: LXX. Nihil ergo pejus hac in parte sentiunt Remonstrantes illis qui Lutherani dicuntur; ac proinde cum Reformati communionem horum non refugiant, sed ultro eos ad pacem & concordiam fraternam invitent, non debent Remonstrantes propter hoc doctrinae caput, si nihil gravius errent, a communione sua repellere; sed eorum hac in re sententiam habere pro tolerabili, & quae pietati perniciosa non sit.
latin.2653: LXXI. Si quis etiam comparet quae Thesibus superioribus de Molina retulimus, cum Remonstrantium doctrina hisce Thesibus exposita, manifesto apparebit, Remonstrantes de gratiae efficacia & sufficientia, reipsa non aliud sentire quam plurimos Scholae Romanae doctores qui Molinam hodie sequuntur. Nempe utrique consentiunt ex duobus hominibus aequali gratia praeventis unum posse converti, alterum non converti, quia unus gratiae obicem libere posuerit, alter non posuerit. Et illis ipsis qui non convertuntur Deum communicare auxilia gratiae ad ipsorum conversionem tam abunde sufficientia, ut ex parte Dei nihil amplius praerequiratur, ad hoc ut reapse sequatur eorum conversio.
latin.2654: LXXII. Nec minus quoque manifestum fecimus illos qui Synodo Dordracenae subscribunt, cum Thomistis recentioribus, & cum illis etiam qui Jansenio adhaerent idem, quoad rei summam, sentire & docere, circa doctrinam de gratia efficaci & sufficienti; & si quibus in rebus dissentire videantur, contentionem vel esse verbalem, vel non admodum momentosam.
latin.2655: LXXIII. Etenim Reformati qui Synodum illam probant, cum istis Scholae Romanae Doctoribus fatentur & agnoscunt, illos qui per Dei gratiam convertuntur, conversionis actus libere elicere, & gratiam Divinam praestare quidem infallibiliter ut credant & resipiscant, sed modo tamen qui sit naturae rationali & liberae consentaneus, & sic ut ab iis simpliciter non tollat potestatem aliter agendi, & pios illos actus omittendi.
latin.2656: LXXIV. Ultro etiam concedunt, illis ipsis qui Evangelium audientes non convertuntur, neque peccato renunciant, praeter externam praedicationis gratiam, multa interna gratiae auxilia communicari, Deumque variis modis intus cor eorum pulsare, & mentem illustrare, ut a peccato recedant, & eam quam par est fidem Evangelio adhibeant: ita ut propria tantum culpa pereant, & per solam eorum perversitatem & contumaciam stet, quin salutis fiant participes.
latin.2657: LXXV. Vicissim vero tam qui Jansenistae vocantur, quam Thomistae recentiores agnoscunt tantam esse gratiae efficaciam, ut voluntatem ad bonum non solum invitet atque sollicitet, sed potenter etiam flectat & determinet; nec ejus efficaciam a liberi arbitrii consensu esse suspendendam, cum ipsa consensum illum, in iis quos convertit, infallibiliter & insuperabiliter proliciat atque efficiat.
latin.2658: LXXVI. Nec minus aperte fatentur omnibus illis qui credere renuunt, aut in peccatis indurantur, auxilium aliquod deesse ex parte Dei prorsus necessarium & praerequisitum, ad hoc ut quis actu fidem concipiat, & veram de peccatis poenitentiam agat.
latin.2659: LXXVII. Itaque quod Thomistae recentiores affirmant, illos in quibus gratia non est efficax ad conversionem, nihilominus gratiam sufficientem ad eam habere, id vero Reformati cum Jansenio negant, mera logomachia est. Siquidem Thomistae per hoc affirmare non intendunt, iis qui non convertuntur nullum deesse auxilium ad eorum conversionem ex parte Dei antecedaneum, quod unice negare volunt Jansenius & Reformati, quum dicunt illos non habere gratiam sufficientem, Thomistis alioqui facile concessuri gratiam quae talibus datur, secundum quid & in suo genere sufficientem dici posse.
latin.2660: LXXVIII. Hoc praesertim videre est in judicio Theologorum Nassovio-Wateravicorum circa tertium & quartum articulum, quod habetur in actis Synodi Dordracenae. Ibi enim explicantes suam Thesin de intentione Dei in hominis vocatione, dicunt gratiam praedicationis & illuminationis, quae hypocritis cum piis communis est, ad conversionem secundum quid sufficientem esse, hoc est, in ordine causarum secundarum, seu mediorum; quatenus nulla alia conversionis media, sive externae praedicationis, sive internae illuminationis, praeter illa requiruntur: Sed non esse sufficientem ad conversionem simpliciter, hoc est, sine internae tractionis gratia; sine qua quenquam converti & ad Christum venire Scriptura pronunciat impossibile.
latin.2661: LXXIX. Quod vero discrimen est inter Thomistas atque Jansenium, & inter ipsos Scholae Reformatae Doctores, in explicanda natura gratiae efficacis, & definiendo qua in re illa constituenda sit, dum illam ponunt Thomistae in motione quadam virtuosa, quae est in voluntate per modum quo impetus in re quae impellitur, Jansenius in affectibus amoris & desiderii boni coelestis & spiritualis, quibus suaviter sursum rapitur animus humanus, discipuli Cameronis in potentissima mentis illuminatione & persuasione quae voluntatem & affectus secum rapit, alii in omnipotenti & efficacissima Dei operatione qua novum principium spiritualis vitae cordi hominis vocati inditur, & homo simul excitatur ad hujus vitae actus eliciendos, res est quae ad disputationem mere Scholasticam pertinet, & de qua viris doctis sic & sic loqui, & opinari licet: & quae hic plerique viri docti proferunt componenda potius quam opponenda videntur.
latin.2662: LXXX. Caeterum tanta varietas sententiarum & opinionum circa naturam atque essentiam gratiae efficacis, & rationem ac modum quo in animis hominum operatur, quae a tot jam saeculis Scholas Christianas exercet, arguit rem esse perplexam, obscuram, & quae undique multis difficultatibus scatet: Nec spes est fore contentionum finem, nisi curiositati modus aliquis statuatur, & omittantur quaestiones arduae & non necessariae. Ac profecto longe consultius foret, & paci ac pietati Christianae conducibilius in totum ab ejusmodi quaestionibus abstinere, quam sine fine rixari de rebus, quae difficultate sua ingenium humanum obruunt, & in quibus vix quisquam sibi potest satisfacere.
latin.2663: LXXXI. Praesertim quaestiones illae apud plebem Christianam, in homiliis & concionibus, non tantum nullo cum fructu, sed maximo saepe cum damno proponuntur, dum simplicium animis injiciuntur varii scrupuli, quos disputantium ars & eloquentia satis postea discutere non potest. Proinde tutissimum esset, & Christianae prudentiae ac sobrietati maxime conveniens, dum de rebus istis sermo apud populum praecipue habetur, in iis consistere de quibus Christiani Doctores conveniunt, & quae sufficiunt quoque ad pietatem & fidem informandam. Qualia sunt quicquid boni nobis inest, & a nobis fit Divinae gratiae deberi. Deum esse qui omne bonum in nobis operatur. Sine Christo & spiritus illius auxilio in iis quae aeternam nostram salutem promovent, nihil nos quicquam posse. Nihil esse quod a Deo gratis non acceperimus, & de quo possimus supra alium gloriari. Adeoque teneri nos in omnibus Dei gratiam implorare, & si quid a nobis bene & recte factum fuerit, de eo illi gratias agere.
latin.2664: LXXXII. Deum tamen qui naturae nostrae author & conditor est, & qua ratione animus humanus movendus sit optime novit, sic per gratiam suam in nobis operari, ut libertati nostrae nihil decedat, eumque nos ad bona facienda movere, non tanquam truncos aut stipites, sed ut creaturas rationales decet. Proindeque divinae gratiae necessitatem atque efficaciam nulla ex parte tollere nostram ad bona opera curam & sollicitudinem: nec minus propterea nobis laborandum & vigilandum esse, quod in omnibus Dei auxilio egemus. Quantacunque vero sit gratiae necessitas, impios qui male agunt, & verbo Dei parere recusant, nullam occasionem habere de Deo querendi. Deum enim sic eos invitare ad resipiscentiam, & illis ea ad salutem media subministrare, ut propria culpa tantum in perditionem ruant, & eorum duntaxat contumaciae & rebellioni tribuendum sit quod salutem aeternam non adipiscantur.
latin.2665: LXXXIII. Ista quae nullus in dubium vocat, Christianis omnibus meo judicio sufficere deberent, absque ulteriori & curiosiori investigatione, tum intimae naturae libertatis humanae, tum modi quo gratia in nobis operatur, & quo etiam ejus efficacia cum arbitrii nostri libertate concilianda est; de quibus nulla diserta, clara, & expressa extant Scripturae oracula. Si quis tamen pertendat licere de his rebus ulterius & accuratius in Scholis Philosophari, optandum saltem esset id fieri summa cum animi moderatione, & agnitione syncera propriae nostrae caliginis atque ignorantiae in rebus tam arduis quae omnem ex disputationibus, circa materiam per se tam gravem atque difficilem, acerbitatem tolleret, & animos ad mutuam Christianam & fraternam tolerantiam formaret. Quod Deus per eandem illam suam gratiam in iis qui Scholis Christianis praesunt, praestare velit.
latin.2666: LXXXIV. Appendicis loco subnectere visum est quid auxiliis gratiae divinae in hominis conversione, & pietatis negotio tribuant hodierni Sociniani. Supponunt igitur hominis voluntatem per naturam peccato sic astrictam non esse, quin possit velle aut nolle aliquid facere, in rebus ad religionem salutemque aeternam spectantibus, & porro etiam, ubi Evangelicam doctrinam auribus perceperit, reipsa credere ac Dei praeceptis parere: Deum enim voluisse ut voluntas nostra, ex qua vitae pietas proficiscitur, & aestimatur, in nostro arbitrio & potestate sita esset: licet interim externum ipsius actum vel promovere, vel impedire, vel permittere pro arbitrio soleat: Unde concludunt velle bonum quod nobis inest, nostrum esse non Dei.
latin.2667: LXXXV. Quod si quis objiciat, si res ita se habet, multum de Dei gubernatione, quae in mundo regendo cernitur, detractum iri: respondent, internum voluntatis nostrae actum, quem solum ordinarie in nostra potestate Deus collocavit, in mundi gubernatione nullum habere momentum, sed externum ejus effectum, qui in Dei potestate ita situs est, ut nihil nisi Deo decernente, juvanteque, aut permittente fieri queat. Liberum autem arbitrium eousque vim suam porrigere, ut Deo nunc juvante, nunc permittente tantum, homo non solum de re quapiam peragenda cogitationem suscipere, sed etiam exitu eam complere possit.
latin.2668: LXXXVI. Speciatim quod ad bonas actiones attinet a voluntate imperatas, quas Deus vult a nobis perfici, agnoscunt illas saepissime absque Dei auxilio fieri non posse. Quod tamen non obstare putant quominus suo modo sint in nostra potestate. Idque quia Deus suum auxilium nulli homini suppliciter ad ipsum accedenti denegat. Adeoque si quis divino auxilio destitutus, illius praeceptis non obtemperaverit, is sibi culpam assignare debet, & sic nullam habet peccati excusationem: propterea quod Dei opem serio non imploravit: aut quae Deus illi ad pietatem colendam suppeditavit adjumenta noluit amplecti. Quod malum nonnisi ab hominis ipsius improbitate fluit. Hinc enim fit ut voluntatem suam ad ea non accommodet quae Deo probantur: quod si faceret, nullum dubium esset, quin ea perficiendi omnem viam rationemque tentaret, & quod consequens est, ad divinam opem nunquam non confugeret, & sic ea circumseptus facile & rerum divinarum scientiam assequeretur, & in Dei studio totam mentem suam defigeret.
latin.2669: LXXXVII. Caeterum duplici ratione Deum hominum conatibus opitulari dicunt; quarum altera externa est, & vel in minando, vel in promittendo consistit: quanquam in promissis major vis sit homines Dei studio inflammandi: altera vero internum auxilium est quod tunc nobis Deus affert, quum vel promissa nobis facta, ac externis documentis confirmata animis nostris divina virtute penitius insculpit, vel pleniori voluntatis suae notitia nos instruit.
latin.2670: LXXXVIII. Quod si quis dicat ipsum velle nostrum, non minus quam opus externum, quum de salutari bono quaestio est, Deo in Scriptura tribui, juxta illud Pauli ad Philippenses. Deus est qui operatur in vobis & velle & perficere pro bona voluntate: Respondent istis verbis & similibus quibus Deo tribuitur hominis conversio, non significari Deum omnino & necessario in hominibus efficere quod verba sonant: sed Deum nihil eorum omittere quae ad id efficiendum, libertate voluntatis nostrae salva, pertineant. Nimirum quia Deus nos ad bonum volendum allicit & invitat beneficiorum magnitudine, & promissionum tum certitudine, tum summa praestantia atque amplitudine, quibus efficit, non ut velle possimus, quod nobis naturaliter inest, sed ut reipsa velimus: quod tamen efficit ea ratione, ut semper in nostra potestate situm sit efficaciae isti divinae resistere. Quae pluribus diducta videre est apud Volkelium Socinianum, De vera Religione libro quinto capite decimo octavo.

sections.title: Remonstrants and Augsburg theologians agree in substance
sections.pass_a: LXVII. Further, from those things which have been set out so far, it is easy to gather that the Remonstrants, & the Theologians of the Augsburg confession, concerning the doctrine of sufficient and efficacious grace, differ indeed to some extent in method & in formulas of speaking, but as to the substance of the matter there is agreement between them. Namely the Theologians of the Augsburg confession deny that grace is rightly divided into efficacious & sufficient, but the Remonstrants affirm it, & approve that distinction very much. But the mind of the Theologians of the Augsburg confession is not that to those who hearing the Word of God are not converted, some help is lacking on God's part without which they cannot be converted; and so that the grace which is given & offered to them, by no means suffices to beget faith & repentance in them. For on the contrary they assert that the grace which is offered to those unbelieving & impenitent people deserves the name not only of sufficient, but also of efficacious: since of itself it is efficacious for bringing them to repentance & faith, unless they go on of their own accord to put an obstacle in the way.
pass_b: Thesis LXVII. From what has been set out so far it is easy to conclude that the Remonstrants and the theologians of the Augsburg Confession differ somewhat in method and in their ways of speaking about sufficient and efficacious grace, but agree on the substance.

The Augsburg theologians deny that grace is properly divided into efficacious and sufficient; the Remonstrants affirm it and strongly approve the distinction. Yet the Augsburg theologians do not mean that those who hear God's Word and are not converted lack some help on God's part without which they cannot be converted; nor, therefore, that the grace given and offered them falls short of producing faith and repentance in them.

On the contrary, they say that the grace offered to these unbelieving and impenitent people deserves to be called not only sufficient but efficacious too, because of itself it is efficacious to bring them to repentance and faith, unless they go on of their own accord putting an obstacle in its way.

sections.title: Why the Remonstrants call such grace merely sufficient
sections.pass_a: LXVIII. But on the other hand the Remonstrants do not distinguish grace into sufficient and efficacious for this reason, that they think the grace which those receive who remain unbelieving, & persevere in sins, does not have the force & efficacy necessary & prerequisite for this, that conversion should follow in them, and therefore deserves only the name of sufficient, but not also of efficacious. For they acknowledge that those who reject the Gospel preached to them, lack no help necessary for conceiving faith; but they deny the name of efficacious to the grace of which they are partakers only for this reason, that it does not actually produce in them the effect for which it is destined, because of the hindrance which men of that kind put in its way, not because the necessary force & efficacy is lacking to grace itself.
pass_b: Thesis LXVIII. The Remonstrants, for their part, do not divide grace into sufficient and efficacious because they think that the grace received by those who stay unbelieving and go on in their sins lacks the force and efficacy needed beforehand for their conversion to follow, so that it earns only the name 'sufficient' and not 'efficacious'.

They grant that those who reject the Gospel preached to them lack no help they need to come to faith. They refuse the name 'efficacious' to the grace these people share in for one reason only: it does not in fact produce in them the effect it is meant for, because of the hindrance such people set up, not because grace itself lacks the force and efficacy required.

sections.title: What both sides confess
sections.pass_a: LXIX. Both therefore confess & teach that the grace which is given to those who refuse to obey the Gospel, has strength enough for converting them, & that it fails to obtain its effect in them only because they resist its motions, & voluntarily put an obstacle in its way. On the other side that the faithful & those who are seriously converted to God, could, if they had pleased, have put an obstacle in the way of the grace which is efficacious in them, & hindered its effect by their obstinacy, nor was any necessity of believing, & of converting themselves to God, imposed on them through that grace.
pass_b: Thesis LXIX. So both sides confess and teach that the grace given to those who will not obey the Gospel has enough strength to convert them, and that it fails to take effect in them only because they resist its motions and willingly put an obstacle in its way.

Conversely, they hold that believers, and those who are converted to God in earnest, could have blocked the grace that is efficacious in them if they had wished, and could have hindered its effect by their obstinacy, and that this grace laid on them no necessity of believing and turning to God.

sections.title: The Remonstrants' view is tolerable
sections.pass_a: LXX. Therefore the Remonstrants think nothing worse in this part than those who are called Lutherans; and accordingly since the Reformed do not shun communion with these, but of their own accord invite them to peace & brotherly concord, the Reformed ought not, on account of this head of doctrine, if they err in nothing more grave, to repel the Remonstrants from their communion; but ought to hold their opinion in this matter as tolerable, & as not pernicious to piety.
pass_b: Thesis LXX. On this point, then, the Remonstrants think nothing worse than those called Lutherans. The Reformed do not avoid communion with the Lutherans; they even invite them, unasked, to peace and brotherly concord.

So, unless the Remonstrants err in something more serious, the Reformed should not shut them out of their communion over this head of doctrine, but should regard their opinion on it as tolerable and not harmful to piety.

sections.title: The Remonstrants and the Molinists agree
sections.pass_a: LXXI. If anyone also compares what we reported in the earlier Theses about Molina, with the doctrine of the Remonstrants set out in these Theses, it will plainly appear that the Remonstrants in fact think nothing other about the efficacy & sufficiency of grace than very many doctors of the Roman School who today follow Molina. Namely both agree that of two men prevented by equal grace one can be converted, the other not converted, because the one freely put an obstacle to grace, the other did not. And that to those very people who are not converted God communicates helps of grace so abundantly sufficient for their conversion, that on God's part nothing more is prerequired, for their conversion actually to follow.
pass_b: Thesis LXXI. Anyone who compares what we reported about Molina in earlier theses with the Remonstrant doctrine set out in these will see clearly that on the efficacy and sufficiency of grace the Remonstrants hold in fact just what many teachers of the Roman school who follow Molina today hold.

Both agree that of two people given equal preventing grace, one can be converted and the other not, because one freely put an obstacle in grace's way and the other did not. Both agree, too, that God gives even those who are not converted helps of grace so fully sufficient for their conversion that nothing more is needed beforehand on God's side for their conversion actually to follow.

sections.title: Dort, the recent Thomists and the Jansenists agree
sections.pass_a: LXXII. No less also have we made it plain that those who subscribe to the Synod of Dort, with the more recent Thomists, & with those also who adhere to Jansenius, think & teach the same, as to the substance of the matter, concerning the doctrine of efficacious & sufficient grace; & if they seem to disagree in some things, the dispute is either verbal, or not of much moment.
pass_b: Thesis LXXII. We have shown just as clearly that those who subscribe to the Synod of Dort think and teach in substance the same thing on efficacious and sufficient grace as the more recent Thomists and the followers of Jansenius.
Where they seem to disagree on some points, the dispute is either about words or of little weight.

sections.title: What the Reformed grant with these Roman doctors
sections.pass_a: LXXIII. For the Reformed who approve that Synod, with those Doctors of the Roman School confess & acknowledge, that those who are converted through the grace of God, freely elicit the acts of conversion, & that divine grace indeed brings it about infallibly that they believe & repent, but yet in a manner which is agreeable to a rational & free nature, & such that it does not absolutely take away from them the power of acting otherwise, & of omitting those pious acts.
pass_b: Thesis LXXIII. The Reformed who approve that Synod confess and acknowledge, together with these teachers of the Roman school, that those converted by God's grace perform the acts of conversion freely.

They hold that God's grace does make sure, infallibly, that they believe and repent, yet in a way that suits a rational and free nature, one that does not take away from them absolutely the power to act otherwise and to leave those devout acts undone.

sections.title: The Reformed grant inward helps to the unconverted
sections.pass_a: LXXIV. They also grant freely, that to those very people who hearing the Gospel are not converted, nor renounce sin, besides the external grace of preaching, many internal helps of grace are communicated, & that God in various ways knocks inwardly at their heart, & illuminates the mind, that they may withdraw from sin, & give to the Gospel the faith which is due: so that they perish only by their own fault, & it is only through their perversity & obstinacy that they do not become partakers of salvation.
pass_b: Thesis LXXIV. They also freely grant that those who hear the Gospel and are not converted or do not give up sin receive, besides the outward grace of preaching, many inward helps of grace. God knocks at their hearts from within in various ways and enlightens their minds, so that they may turn from sin and give the Gospel the faith it deserves.
So they perish only through their own fault, and it is their perversity and obstinacy alone that keeps them from sharing in salvation.

sections.title: Jansenists and recent Thomists on efficacious grace
sections.pass_a: LXXV. But in turn both those who are called Jansenists, and the more recent Thomists, acknowledge that the efficacy of grace is so great, that it not only invites & solicits the will to good, but also powerfully bends & determines it; and that its efficacy is not to be suspended on the consent of free choice, since it itself draws forth & effects that consent, in those whom it converts, infallibly & insuperably.
pass_b: Thesis LXXV. In turn, both the so-called Jansenists and the more recent Thomists acknowledge that grace is so efficacious that it does not merely invite and urge the will toward the good but also bends and determines it with power.

Its efficacy, they say, is not to be made to hang on the consent of free choice, since in those it converts grace itself draws out and produces that consent, infallibly and in a way that cannot be overcome.

pass_b: Thesis LXXVI. They admit just as openly that everyone who refuses to believe or is hardened in sin lacks some help on God's part that is entirely necessary, and needed beforehand, if a person is actually to come to faith and truly repent of his sins.

sections.title: The dispute over 'sufficient grace' is verbal
sections.pass_a: LXXVII. And so, that the more recent Thomists affirm that those in whom grace is not efficacious for conversion nevertheless have grace sufficient for it, but the Reformed with Jansenius deny it, is a mere dispute about words. For the Thomists by this do not intend to affirm, that to those who are not converted no antecedent help on God's part is lacking for their conversion, which alone Jansenius & the Reformed mean to deny, when they say that those people do not have sufficient grace, being otherwise ready easily to grant the Thomists that the grace which is given to such people can be called sufficient in a certain respect & in its own kind.
pass_b: Thesis LXXVII. The recent Thomists hold that people in whom grace fails to convert nonetheless possess grace sufficient for conversion; the Reformed, siding with Jansenius, reject this. The quarrel is purely verbal.

What the Thomists intend is not the claim that the unconverted are missing no help from God that would have to come first. Only that claim is what Jansenius and the Reformed reject in saying such people lack sufficient grace. Apart from it, they would happily concede to the Thomists that the grace these people receive may be termed sufficient after a fashion, within its own kind.

sections.title: The Nassau-Wetterau theologians at Dort
sections.pass_a: LXXVIII. This may be seen especially in the judgment of the Nassau-Wetterau Theologians on the third & fourth article, which is found in the acts of the Synod of Dort. For there, explaining their Thesis on the intention of God in the calling of man, they say that the grace of preaching & illumination, which is common to hypocrites with the godly, is sufficient for conversion in a certain respect, that is, in the order of second causes, or of means; inasmuch as no other means of conversion, whether of external preaching, or of internal illumination, are required besides those: But that it is not sufficient for conversion absolutely, that is, without the grace of internal drawing; without which Scripture pronounces it impossible that anyone be converted & come to Christ.
pass_b: Thesis LXXVIII. A clear case is the Nassau-Wetterau theologians' judgment on the third and fourth articles, preserved in the Acts of the Synod of Dort. In setting out their thesis on what God intends when he calls people, they grant that preaching and enlightenment, a grace hypocrites have in common with the godly, suffices for conversion in one respect: at the level of secondary causes or means, in that conversion requires no further means beyond these, whether of outward preaching or of inward enlightenment.

Taken without qualification, though, it does not suffice, that is, without the grace of being drawn from within; and without that grace, Scripture declares, it is impossible for anyone to be converted and come to Christ.

sections.title: Differences on the nature of efficacious grace are scholastic
sections.pass_a: LXXIX. But the difference there is between the Thomists and Jansenius, & among the Doctors of the Reformed School themselves, in explaining the nature of efficacious grace, & in defining in what it is to be placed, while the Thomists place it in a certain virtuous motion, which is in the will in the way an impetus is in a thing which is impelled, Jansenius in affections of love & of desire of the heavenly & spiritual good, by which the human mind is sweetly carried upward, the disciples of Camero in a most powerful illumination & persuasion of the mind which carries the will & affections with it, others in an omnipotent & most efficacious operation of God by which a new principle of spiritual life is put into the heart of the man called, & the man at the same time is stirred to elicit the acts of this life, is a matter which belongs to merely Scholastic disputation, & about which learned men may speak & hold opinions this way & that: & what most learned men here put forward seems to be reconciled rather than opposed.
pass_b: Thesis LXXIX. There are differences between the Thomists and Jansenius, and among the teachers of the Reformed school themselves, over how to explain the nature of efficacious grace and in what to place it.

The Thomists place it in a certain motion with power in it, present in the will as an impetus is present in a thing that is driven; Jansenius in feelings of love and longing for the heavenly and spiritual good, by which the human soul is gently swept upward; Camero's disciples in a most powerful enlightening and persuading of the mind, which sweeps the will and affections along with it; others in an all-powerful and most effective working of God, by which a new source of spiritual life is put into the heart of the person called and he is at the same time roused to perform the acts of this life.

All this belongs to purely scholastic debate, on which learned men may speak and think one way or another; and what most learned men put forward here seems to call for reconciling rather than setting against each other.

sections.title: A plea to leave arduous questions aside
sections.pass_a: LXXX. Moreover so great a variety of opinions & views about the nature and essence of efficacious grace, & the reason and manner in which it works in the souls of men, which has now for so many centuries exercised the Christian Schools, shows that the matter is perplexed, obscure, & one that teems on every side with many difficulties: Nor is there hope that there will be an end of the disputes, unless some limit is set to curiosity, & arduous & unnecessary questions are left aside. And indeed it would be far more advisable, & more conducive to Christian peace and piety, to abstain wholly from questions of that kind, than to quarrel without end about things, which by their difficulty overwhelm the human mind, & in which scarcely anyone can satisfy himself.
pass_b: Thesis LXXX. The great variety of opinions and views on the nature and essence of efficacious grace, and on how it works in people's souls, which has occupied the Christian schools for so many centuries now, shows that the matter is tangled and obscure and full of difficulties on every side.

There is no hope that the disputes will end unless some limit is put to curiosity and hard, unnecessary questions are dropped. It would indeed be far wiser, and better for Christian peace and piety, to keep away from such questions altogether than to quarrel endlessly over matters that overwhelm the human mind by their difficulty and on which hardly anyone can satisfy himself.

sections.title: What should be preached to the people
sections.pass_a: LXXXI. Especially those questions are put before the Christian people, in homilies & sermons, not only with no fruit, but often with very great harm, while various scruples are thrown into the minds of the simple, which the art & eloquence of the disputants cannot afterwards sufficiently dispel. Accordingly it would be safest, & most agreeable to Christian prudence and sobriety, while discourse on those things is held especially before the people, to keep to those things on which Christian Doctors agree, & which also suffice for forming piety & faith. Such are that whatever good is in us, & is done by us is owed to Divine grace. That it is God who works every good in us. That without Christ & the help of his spirit we can do nothing at all in those things which promote our eternal salvation. That there is nothing which we have not received freely from God, & about which we can glory over another. And so that we are bound in all things to implore the grace of God, & if anything has been done well & rightly by us, to give him thanks for it.
pass_b: Thesis LXXXI. These questions in particular are brought before ordinary Christians in homilies and sermons not only to no profit but often to great harm, since they plant scruples in simple minds that the skill and eloquence of the disputants cannot properly clear away afterwards.

So when these matters are spoken of, especially before the people, the safest course, and the one that best suits Christian prudence and sobriety, would be to keep to what Christian teachers agree on, which is also enough to shape piety and faith.

For example: whatever good is in us and is done by us is owed to God's grace; it is God who works all good in us; without Christ and the help of his Spirit we can do nothing at all in what furthers our eternal salvation; we have nothing that we have not received freely from God and could boast of over another; and so we must ask for God's grace in everything, and thank him for whatever we have done well and rightly.

sections.title: Grace leaves freedom and effort intact; the wicked have no excuse
sections.pass_a: LXXXII. That yet God, who is the author & founder of our nature, & knows best in what way the human mind is to be moved, so works in us through his grace, that nothing is taken from our freedom, & moves us to doing good things, not as trunks or stocks, but as befits rational creatures. And accordingly that the necessity and efficacy of divine grace in no part takes away our care & diligence for good works: nor must we labour & watch any the less on this account, that in all things we need the help of God. But however great the necessity of grace, the wicked who do evil, & refuse to obey the word of God, have no occasion to complain of God. For God so invites them to repentance, & supplies them with those means to salvation, that they rush into perdition only by their own fault, & it is to be attributed only to their obstinacy & rebellion that they do not obtain eternal salvation.
pass_b: Thesis LXXXII. Yet God, the author and maker of our nature, who knows best how the human soul is to be moved, works in us by his grace in such a way that our freedom loses nothing, and he moves us to do good not as if we were logs or posts but as befits rational creatures.
So the necessity and efficacy of God's grace in no way remove our care and concern for good works, and we must not work and watch any less because we need God's help in everything.

However necessary grace is, the wicked who do evil and refuse to obey God's word have no grounds for complaint against God. He invites them to repentance and gives them the means of salvation in such a way that they rush to ruin only through their own fault, and their failure to gain eternal salvation must be put down to their obstinacy and rebellion alone.

sections.title: Enough for Christians; moderation in the schools
sections.pass_a: LXXXIII. Those things which no one calls in doubt, ought in my judgment to suffice all Christians, without further & more curious investigation, both of the inmost nature of human freedom, and of the manner in which grace works in us, & in which also its efficacy is to be reconciled with the freedom of our choice; about which there exist no distinct, clear, & express oracles of Scripture. Yet if anyone maintains that it is lawful to philosophize about these things further & more exactly in the Schools, it would at least be desirable that it be done with the greatest moderation of mind, & sincere acknowledgment of our own darkness and ignorance in things so arduous which would take away all bitterness from disputes, on a matter in itself so weighty and difficult, & would form minds to mutual Christian & brotherly toleration. Which may God be pleased to bring about through that same grace of his in those who preside over the Christian Schools.
pass_b: Thesis LXXXIII. In my judgment these points, which no one questions, ought to be enough for all Christians, without further and more curious inquiry into the inmost nature of human freedom, into how grace works in us, or into how its efficacy is to be reconciled with the freedom of our choice; on these Scripture gives no distinct, clear and express pronouncements.

If anyone insists that it is permissible to philosophize about these matters further and more precisely in the schools, it would at least be desirable to do so with the greatest restraint, and with a sincere admission of our own darkness and ignorance in such hard matters. That would take all bitterness out of the debates on a subject so weighty and difficult in itself, and would train minds to mutual Christian and brotherly tolerance. May God, by that same grace of his, be pleased to bring this about in those who preside over the Christian schools.

sections.title: Appendix: the Socinians on grace
sections.pass_a: LXXXIV. By way of appendix it has seemed good to subjoin what the Socinians of today attribute to the helps of divine grace in the conversion of man, & in the business of piety. They suppose then that the will of man is not by nature so bound by sin, that it cannot will or not will to do something, in things that look to religion and eternal salvation, & further also, when it has heard the Evangelical doctrine with the ears, actually believe and obey the precepts of God: For God willed that our will, from which the piety of life proceeds, & is reckoned, should be placed in our choice & power: although meanwhile he is wont to promote, or hinder, or permit its external act at his choice: Whence they conclude that the willing of good which is in us, is ours not God's.
pass_b: Thesis LXXXIV. By way of appendix, it seemed right to add what the Socinians of today ascribe to the helps of God's grace in a person's conversion and in the practice of piety. They assume that the human will is not so bound by sin by nature that it cannot will or refuse to do something in matters of religion and eternal salvation, and also, once a person has heard the Gospel teaching, actually believe and obey God's commands.

God, they say, willed that our will, from which piety of life springs and by which it is judged, should lie within our choice and power, though he commonly furthers, hinders or permits its outward act as he chooses. From this they conclude that the willing of good that is in us is ours, not God's.

sections.title: Socinians: God's government and the inward act
sections.pass_a: LXXXV. But if anyone objects, if the matter is so, that much will be taken away from the government of God, which is seen in ruling the world: they answer, that the internal act of our will, which alone God has ordinarily placed in our power, has no weight in the government of the world, but its external effect does, which is so placed in God's power, that nothing can be done except with God decreeing, & helping, or permitting. But that free choice extends its force so far, that with God now helping, now only permitting, man can not only undertake the thought of carrying out some thing, but also complete it in outcome.
pass_b: Thesis LXXXV. If anyone objects that on this view much will be taken away from God's government as seen in his ruling of the world, they answer that the inward act of our will, the only thing God has ordinarily put in our power, carries no weight in the government of the world.

What matters there is its outward effect, which is so subject to God's power that nothing can happen unless God decrees and helps, or permits it. Free choice reaches far enough, they say, that with God sometimes helping and sometimes only permitting, a person can not only conceive a plan to do something but carry it through to the end.

sections.title: Socinians: God's help is never refused to those who ask
sections.pass_a: LXXXVI. Specially as regards good actions commanded by the will, which God wills to be accomplished by us, they acknowledge that they very often cannot be done without the help of God. Which yet they think does not prevent their being in their own way in our power. And that because God denies his help to no man approaching him as a suppliant. And so if anyone destitute of divine help has not obeyed his precepts, he must assign the blame to himself, & so has no excuse for sin: because he did not seriously implore the help of God: or would not embrace the aids which God supplied him for practising piety. Which evil flows only from the man's own wickedness. For hence it comes about that he does not fit his will to those things which are approved by God: which if he did, there would be no doubt, but that he would try every way and means of accomplishing them, & what is consequent, would never fail to take refuge in divine help, & so, hedged about by it, would easily both attain knowledge of divine things, & fix his whole mind on zeal for God.
pass_b: Thesis LXXXVI. As for good actions that the will commands and God wants us to carry out, they grant that these very often cannot be done without God's help. They do not think this prevents them from being in our power in their own way, because God refuses his help to no one who comes to him as a suppliant.

So if someone without God's help has not obeyed his commands, he must blame himself and has no excuse for his sin, because he did not earnestly ask for God's help, or would not take up the aids God gave him for practising piety. That evil comes only from the person's own wickedness, which makes him not bring his will into line with what God approves.

If he did, there would be no doubt that he would try every way and means of carrying it out, and would therefore always turn to God's help; protected by it, he would easily gain knowledge of divine things and fix his whole mind on devotion to God.

Moreover they say that God aids the endeavours of men in a twofold way; of which the one is external, & consists either in threatening, or in promising: although in the promises there is greater force for inflaming men with zeal for God: but the other is an internal help which God then brings us, when he either engraves more deeply on our minds by divine power the promises made to us, and confirmed by external proofs, or instructs us with a fuller knowledge of his will.
pass_b: Thesis LXXXVII. They say, further, that God aids human efforts in two ways. One is outward and lies in threats or in promises, though promises have more power to fire people with devotion to God.
The other is an inward help that God gives us when, by divine power, he engraves more deeply on our minds the promises made to us and confirmed by outward proofs, or teaches us his will more fully.

sections.title: Socinians on Philippians 2:13
sections.pass_a: LXXXVIII. But if anyone says that our willing itself, no less than the external work, when the question is about saving good, is attributed in Scripture to God, according to that saying of Paul to the Philippians. It is God who works in you both to will & to accomplish according to his good pleasure: They answer that by these words & similar ones by which the conversion of man is attributed to God, it is not signified that God altogether & necessarily effects in men what the words sound: but that God omits none of those things which pertain to effecting it, the freedom of our will remaining safe. Namely because God entices & invites us to will the good by the greatness of his benefits, & by both the certainty, and the highest excellence and amplitude of his promises, by which he brings it about, not that we can will, which is in us naturally, but that we actually will: which yet he brings about in such a way, that it is always placed in our power to resist that divine efficacy. Which may be seen set out more fully in Volkelius the Socinian, On true Religion book five chapter eighteen.
pass_b: Thesis LXXXVIII. Someone may say that where saving good is concerned Scripture ascribes to God our very willing, no less than the outward deed, as in Paul's words to the Philippians: 'It is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish, for his good pleasure.'

They answer that these words, and others like them that ascribe a person's conversion to God, do not mean that God wholly and necessarily brings about in people what the words say, but that God leaves out nothing that serves to bring it about while our will's freedom stays intact.

God draws and invites us to will the good by the greatness of his gifts and by the certainty, surpassing worth and breadth of his promises. By these he makes us not able to will, which we have by nature, but actually willing; yet he does it in such a way that it always lies in our power to resist that divine efficacy. This is set out more fully in Volkelius the Socinian, On True Religion, book 5, chapter 18.
